We introduce E-GEO as a benchmark for evaluating GEO systems in e-commerce. Its role is to

\text{batch}&c=0&c=1&c=2&c=3&c=4&c=5&c=6\\\hline
0&0.270&0.260&0.250&0.245&0.240&0.235&0.230\\
1&0.275&0.275&0.275&0.275&0.275&0.275&0.250\\
t\geq2&0.250&0.250&0.250&0.250&0.250&0.250&0.250
\end{array}$$
Each row is a nonincreasing survival function, realized by nonnegative score masses between adjacent cuts, with the remaining mass below the lowest cut or above the highest. Every rate lies within the tolerance band. The cut indices may be offsets from a positive threshold $C>1$; shifting the realizing scores and threshold bounds by $C$ preserves the construction and keeps all $H_T$ values nonnegative. The batches are prescribed independently of the actions, and all five increments respect the safety bound.

With Equation (2)'s previous-move penalty, the first rewards for increments $(-2,-1,0,1,2)$ are $(0.52,0.88,1,0.97,0.88)$. Staying at cut $2$ is uniquely greedy. From that cut, no second action reaches cut $6$; the largest second reward is $0.25$. Zero increments thereafter maximize the common continuation. In contrast, increments $(2,2,0,\ldots)$ give rewards $(0.88,0.75,0.75,1,\ldots)$. At $\gamma=0.95$, their advantage over the best continuation after the greedy first action is
$$-0.12+0.95(0.75-0.25)+0.95^2(0.75-1)=\frac{207}{1600}>0.$$
Charging the current increment instead gives first rewards $(0.27,0.755,1,0.845,0.63)$, so staying remains uniquely greedy; the same alternative sequence has a positive discounted advantage of $21/200$. Thus a non-greedy first choice is better under either penalty convention, using the full five-action set and an infinite continuation with every cut inside the rate band.
checks.repair: A general greedy-optimality theorem needs additional assumptions that remove the dependence across decisions. One sufficient setting lets the action choose any absolute threshold from a common set, makes future exogenous state transitions independent of that choice, and omits switching costs. Then the continuation value in the Bellman equation is independent of the chosen threshold, so maximizing the immediate reward is optimal. Those assumptions replace the paper's bounded updates and positive move penalty; they do not establish its exact-optimality claim for the stated controller.
checks.scope: The claim of exact greedy optimality in Section 3.2 is false for the bounded-increment control problem in Equations (1) and (2).
checks.title: Bounded threshold updates can make a non-greedy action optimal
checks.claimContext: The controller changes a threshold $c_t$ by a bounded increment $a_t$, applies the new threshold to the next batch, and receives a reward for background-rate tracking and signal efficiency, with a penalty for threshold changes. Section 3.2 argues that immediate rewards and exogenous beam drift make greedy control optimal for every discount $\gamma$. Its conclusion is that “every $\gamma$ induces the same optimum and $\gamma = 0$ is exact rather than approximate.”
